questions.q: According to the lesson, how many distinct access surfaces typically exist under one model's name, and what are they?
options: Four: training data, model weights/artifacts, the registry entry, and the inference endpoint
One: a single login shared by everyone who touches the model
Two: just the model file and the server it runs on
Four, but all of them should always share the same permission level
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly names four separate surfaces, each with a different blast radius if mishandled.

questions.q: What access does a customer-facing application calling a model for predictions actually need, per the lesson's least-privilege example?
options: Inference access only — no business touching training data or the raw model file
Full administrative access to the model registry
Direct read access to the raw training data
Write access to retrain the model on demand
questions.explain: The lesson specifies inference-only access for this role — anything beyond that is over-granting.

questions.q: In the dashboard example, what caused the unintended data exposure?
options: The dashboard was wired up with a service account that already had full training-data access, because it was convenient, rather than being scoped to only what explaining decisions requires
The dashboard had no access to the model at all
The training data was published publicly on purpose
The model's weights were deleted by mistake
questions.explain: The root cause in the lesson's example is reusing a broad-access account instead of granting the narrow access the explanation feature actually needed.

questions.q: What does the lesson say a risk reviewer approving a model version needs access to?
options: Read access to the registry, documentation, and evaluation results — not the raw training data, and not the ability to modify the model
Full write access to retrain the model themselves
Nothing — reviewers don't need any system access
Only the marketing materials about the model
questions.explain: The lesson scopes a reviewer's access to read-only documentation and results, distinct from a data scientist's or engineer's access.

questions.q: Besides granting the correct access up front, what does the lesson say needs to happen on an ongoing basis?
options: Logging access to training data and weights, reviewing permissions on a cadence tied to risk tier, and revoking access when a role changes
Nothing further — access only needs to be set once
Deleting the model after every permission review
Granting every new employee full access by default to save time
questions.explain: The lesson frames access control as an ongoing practice: logging, periodic review scaled to risk, and revocation on role change, not a one-time setup.
